name: Colin Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Everything here is confidential. What does a normal day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Colin Rossi, twenty-seven, and I lead the small-business returns team at Mill Lane Accounts. I have a master's and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I earn roughly the usual rate. I review tax returns, meet shop owners and builders, and show two apprentices why a figure matters. I use AI checks every day, often before the rest of the office, but I still compare them with invoices.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the day do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like teaching an apprentice how a messy receipt becomes a defensible tax line. The late records and last-minute calls wear me down. Mara and I have about four months of expenses saved and are planning a wedding without debt. There are some similar firms nearby, but I would rather build a service here than commute farther just for a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That is less dramatic than the sales pitch, and I could live with it. I use a checking tool daily at Mill Lane Accounts, but a decent accountant still needs to read the supplier's actual invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the useful bits should be kept and the rest should be dropped. I'd tell the apprentices a shortcut is worth having only when you can explain the answer to the client across a table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally I'd be comfortable. I'm twenty-seven, paid the normal rate for a team lead, and Mara and I have about four months of bills saved. There are a few firms within reach, and our wedding is funded without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the daily AI cross-check on tax returns and the Friday review with the two apprentices I supervise. I'd keep putting two hundred a month into our wedding and emergency account. In the first year of a plateau, I'd ask the partners to keep one apprentice intake because shop owners still bring us confusing records.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Deadlines will still be irritating, but our work and household money should hold steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the tool miss recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One builder brought me a van invoice with the tax split across two pages. The AI missed a tax deduction because the builder's van invoice had a second page. I showed my apprentice how to spot it before calling the builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why push for apprentices if things stay level?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the partners the apprenticeship costs and how many shop accounts we finished with the new starters. If the work stays, I would rather train a young person than buy a bigger license for the tool. Mara and I can keep the wedding date either way.

say: I would keep **useful AI checks** but explain every answer.
I would defend the **apprentice intake** if shop work stays.
think: Our **four-month cushion** makes this future comfortable even while we prepare for the wedding.
The funded **wedding plan** does not depend on new technology.
do: Keep **daily invoice checks** and Friday apprentice reviews.
Save **two hundred monthly** for the wedding and emergencies.
Ask partners to keep the **apprentice intake** if shop demand holds.
feel: I feel **calm** about our work and bills.
S0.quote: The AI missed a tax deduction because the builder's van invoice had a second page.
fieldNote: His **daily tool use** is grounded in finding real invoice mistakes, not a sales promise.
A **funded wedding** and four-month reserve leave him calm, while apprenticeship remains a priority.

steps.text: Keep daily AI invoice checks and Friday apprentice reviews
Save two hundred monthly for wedding and emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture software taking our booking, checking and customer replies. That would make a small practice quicker, but it could also remove the first rung apprentices use to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to compete on price and service, and to spend some of the gains on apprentices. I'd say publicly that work should lead to a trade, not to a waiting room for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could probably run a leaner team, and that is good for the firm, but I might train nobody under me. If a competitor undercuts our fees, my normal salary could come under pressure too. I would not hide that from Mara.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a six-week trial on twenty builder and shop returns using the new review system. I'd teach the apprentices to trace exceptions back to invoices and count errors, not only saved minutes. If the trial cuts enough time, I'd propose a low-fee small-business service and ask the partners to fund the two apprentice places from that income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about pay and the training ladder, though I see a business move. Some nearby firms give me options if this one gets the balance wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who learns when checking becomes automatic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My apprentice Ben has just passed his first exam. I'd give him the odd invoice files because they teach judgment more than clean uploads. A cheap return that produces no future accountants is a short-lived bargain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the new service pay for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The partners would need to see the price, likely one third below our standard return, and the hours to deliver it. I'd present actual trial numbers before asking them to fund the places. If the new service does not sell, I cannot promise the apprentices a wage from it.

say: I would compete on **fees and service** while funding apprentices.
I would insist work offers a **real trade** to learn.
think: A leaner team could erase the **apprentice ladder** that taught me the work.
My own **salary** could be squeezed by cheaper rivals.
do: Trial the **review system** on twenty returns for six weeks.
Teach apprentices to **trace errors** back to invoices.
Pitch a **lower-fee service** only if trial numbers fund apprentice wages.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my salary and the apprentice places.
S1.quote: A cheap return that produces no future accountants is a short-lived bargain.
fieldNote: The **six-week trial** reflects his willingness to use new systems before competitors do.
He makes **apprentice wages** conditional on sales from a cheaper service, not a promise from management.

steps.text: Trial automated review on twenty builder and shop returns
Teach apprentices to trace AI errors back to invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 is not much more than one wedding and two tax seasons away. An accountant that is better and cheaper than me would change every fee proposal in the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to show the books and decide quickly whether the firm can survive. I would tell friends I prefer a job offer or a paying customer to a promise that a new allowance will fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own returns and review work are thinking work, so I expect my job to vanish in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. The robots coming around 2031 do not give my desk another three years. Four months saved and a few nearby firms help less if all those firms face the same price drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the wedding venue deposit and keep its three thousand in cash this month. I'd ask the partners whether they would back a small outsourced bookkeeping service with me, but only invest if two clients sign contracts that cover its basic costs. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I'd take any booked work and apply for a funded accounts-control vacancy outside small practices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Mara and I can delay a party, but I cannot tell her my wage is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara works in a pharmacy and earns less than I do. I'd tell her tonight that the venue deposit can wait while we see whether those clients sign. We would still marry, but perhaps at the town hall with family rather than a large reception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real customer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the two builders who already ask for monthly bookkeeping, then write down the price each would pay. A verbal maybe does not pay for a software license. If neither signs, I keep the three thousand and look for a salaried post.

say: I would ask the firm for **open books** and a survival decision.
I would prefer **paying customers** to vague rescue promises.
think: My **desk role** may end soon after 2028.
Four months saved may not cover a **town-wide price drop**.
do: Delay the **venue deposit** and hold three thousand cash.
Call **two builders** and require signed contracts before investing.
Apply after 2028 for a **funded control vacancy** if my post ends.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing my wage.
S2.quote: A verbal maybe does not pay for a software license.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking deadline** reaches his tax work before robots matter.
His **wedding deposit** becomes a cash reserve, and business investment requires two signed clients.

steps.text: Delay wedding venue deposit and keep three thousand cash
Invest in bookkeeping service only if two clients sign cost-covering contracts
Apply for funded accounts-control vacancy after 2028 if job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to build a customer list before the old return business changes. I would still treat 2031 as a hard date for my desk work, not a reason to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should train apprentices to sell and check a service, not only enter receipts. I'd tell friends I'd rather build a paying practice than depend on a grant whose rules could change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could have a small bookkeeping service by then, but it would have to earn real money. AGI may do the books cheaply in 2031, so the part I sell would be meeting owners, finding bad records and carrying responsibility. Robots in 2034 do not add time to my screen job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd enrol in the six-hundred small-business advisory course if Mill Lane pays the fee and gives me paid study hours. I'd test a monthly records clinic with three builders on Saturdays, but only charge and continue if they value it. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax role ends, I'd extend the clinic only if signed monthly fees cover our rent; otherwise I'd apply for a funded practice-manager vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can work with five years. I would need to see invoices paid, not just encouraging conversations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can afford the course, but I will not quietly subsidise the firm with unpaid nights. I'd put the fee and paid hours in a request to the partners. If they refuse, I'd use the free business centre sessions and postpone the formal qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge the clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three builders are enough to show me whether the clinic solves something. I would record bookings, repeat visits and what they actually pay. I will stop the Saturday records clinic if it becomes a hobby dressed up as a business.

say: I would teach apprentices **client service** as well as checks.
I would require **paid demand** before calling a practice viable.
think: My **tax role** is exposed when full AGI arrives in 2031, whatever I build before then.
A records clinic could work only with **repeat paying clients**.
do: Take **advisory study** with employer-funded fee and paid hours; otherwise attend free business sessions.
Test a **three-builder clinic** and track repeat fees.
Expand after 2031 only if **signed fees** cover rent; otherwise seek a funded vacancy.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but the longer runway helps.
S3.quote: I will stop the Saturday records clinic if it becomes a hobby dressed up as a business.
fieldNote: The **funded course** condition prevents the firm from shifting training costs onto him.
The **clinic test** measures repeat fees, with expansion contingent on rent coverage after 2031.

steps.text: Take advisory course with employer-funded fee and paid study; otherwise attend free business sessions
Test Saturday records clinic with three builders; continue only if paid
Expand records clinic after 2031 only if signed fees cover rent
Apply for funded practice-manager vacancy after 2031 if clinic cannot cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would let me build slowly, which suits a business better than a rush. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, perhaps with a child, though Mara and I have not set that date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives firms time to open apprenticeships that lead somewhere and to let small practices compete. I would oppose locking up the tools for a few large firms, because clients should have a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still expect my tax returns to be automated when AGI reaches thinking work in 2036. The hope is to own a small client service built around trust and clear records by then. Robots around 2039 do not extend the life of the tax desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd put five hundred of our savings into a secure client portal only if Mill Lane permits me to test it on my own time without taking its clients. I'd keep the two-hundred monthly saving transfer and set a date to review the portal's costs next summer. In the first year after 2036, if my accounting post ends, I'd move fully into the service only if signed contracts cover rent and a modest wage; otherwise I'd seek a salaried practice role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than frightened. A decade gives me chances to test a business, but I still need a wage for our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the portal worth building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The portal is not the business; two customers who pay on time would be the business. I would show Mara the receipts before talking about leaving Mill Lane. We have a wedding to pay for before any grand expansion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your firm forbids the side trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the permission in writing so there is no argument about client lists. If the firm says no, I won't spend the five hundred or take a client behind its back. I would use our savings for the wedding and keep looking at jobs.

say: I would protect **small-firm competition** and useful apprenticeships.
I would ask that clients have **real choice** among practices.
think: My **return work** still ends with thinking AI in 2036.
A **client service** needs contracts, not a portal alone.
do: Spend **five hundred** on a portal only with firm permission.
Keep saving **two hundred monthly** while testing demand.
Move after 2036 if **signed contracts** cover rent and a wage; otherwise seek salaried practice vacancies.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because the service still needs paying clients.
S4.quote: The portal is not the business; two customers who pay on time would be the business.
fieldNote: The **portal investment** is conditional on written permission and a defined cost review.
He would leave only with **signed contracts** that cover rent and wages after 2036.

steps.text: Invest five hundred in client portal only with written firm permission
Save two hundred monthly for wedding and emergency account
Move into client service after 2036 if signed contracts cover rent and wage
Seek salaried practice vacancy after 2036 if service contracts cannot cover rent and wage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it hits my desk work before a new customer base can pay the bills. Firm accounts shown to staff, a paid apprenticeship route and an actual vacancy outside tax preparation would help. I would take temporary support if I had to, but I would rather sell a useful service or earn a wage. My partner Mara and I can change the wedding, but we cannot make rent optional.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to apprentices if a firm stops teaching the basics. A practice can buy a system next year, but it cannot buy ten years of judgment back when the last experienced accountant leaves. I worry about who will know an invoice is wrong when the screen looks clean.

headlineQuote: My partner Mara and I can change the wedding, but we cannot make rent optional.
portrait: At **twenty-seven**, Colin leads small-business returns and coaches two apprentices at Mill Lane.
His **master’s** and chartered qualification bring typical pay, with four months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI daily** and checks its output against invoices.
He favours **competition and apprenticeships**, with paid customers and family stability ahead of vague promises.
A **2028 arrival** could end his desk role before a side service earns enough for rent.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his tax role before a new customer base pays the bills.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **open firm accounts**, a paid apprenticeship route and a real vacancy beyond tax preparation.
